 United Airlines says it resolved system outage that delayed flights
 By Danya Gainor , Pete Muntean , Alexandra Skores 
 Updated Nov 16, 2026, 6:07 PM ET 
 PUBLISHED Nov 16, 2026, 5:12 PM ET 
 United Airlines passenger planes are seen at gates at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) in Newark, New Jersey, on November 15, 2026. 
 Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty Images

 [Breaking news update, published at 6:02 p.m. ET] 
 A widespread United Airlines system outage affecting departing flights Monday was resolved, the airline said in a statement, adding that some flights were delayed but there was no impact on flights in progress or on United Express flights.
 [Original story, published November 16, 2026, at 5:12 p.m. ET] 
 United Airlines is experiencing a widespread system outage affecting departing flights and is working to get operations “back up and running as soon as possible,” the airline said in a post on X , just days after a rare FAA ground stop halted all departures nationwide for hours .
 The Federal Aviation Administration is aware of the incident, agency spokesperson Hannah Walden told CNN. The FAA said United was experiencing a technology outage on its end and that “it’s not an FAA equipment issue.”
 United said there is no indication that the outage is a cybersecurity-related issue and that there is no impact on flights in progress or on United Express flights.
 The technology outage is affecting access to multiple applications used by flight crews, according to an internal company alert obtained by CNN.
 The airline instructed pilots not to log out of several systems, warning they may be unable to sign back in. The affected applications include flight planning, weather briefing and crew management tools.
 Pilots unable to access their flight plans are being directed to contact dispatchers to have the documents emailed to them.
 The memo does not disclose the cause of the outage.
 Fourteen percent of United Airlines’ flights were delayed as of 6 p.m. ET Monday, according to the flight-tracking website FlightAware , but not all the delays are necessarily tied to the system outage.
 Air traffic control audio captured by ATC.com shows the moment the outage occurred.
 “Hey, we’re uh, still waiting on our final weights,” a pilot on United Flight 1728 in El Paso, heading to Denver, said to a controller. “We just contacted ops and apparently there’s a company-wide system outage on it so might be a while.”
 The controller responds back, “United 1728, roger, so you don’t have any idea when you think you’ll be able to leave?”
 “No ma’am,” the pilot responds.
 Aviation industry still recovering from weekend ground stop
 The industry had largely returned to normal operations after the ground stop was lifted just after 8 p.m. ET on Friday, though airlines have still worked to reposition planes, crews and luggage as they grappled with the weekend’s score of cancellations and delays .
 Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy held a 45-minute news conference Saturday morning to address the FAA ground stop, and apologized to travelers as he said he was still working to determine what exactly went wrong.
 Duffy told reporters that upgrade work on an old telecommunication system could be a cause for Friday’s nationwide ground stop.
 In at least one remote FAA location, Duffy said contractor L3Harris was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from an old copper wire to fiber, which he described as “straightforward” work that has been happening across the country for decades.
 As United Airlines indicated for Monday’s system outage, Friday’s ground stop didn’t appear to have been caused by a cyber attack or any “nefarious” activity, Duffy stressed at the news conference.
 “A lot of questions came in yesterday. ‘Was this a, a cyber attack? Did some foreign nation attack this network?’ And the answer to that is we don’t believe so,” Duffy said.
 This is a developing story and will be updated.
